questions.question: Define physical change and chemical change, give two examples of each, and state the single question that classifies any change.
questions.expected_answer: A physical change is a change in which no new substance forms: the particles themselves remain unchanged, and only their arrangement, spacing or energy changes, so the change is usually easy to reverse. Examples: melting ice (still water), dissolving salt in water (evaporation returns identical salt), tearing paper, grinding a crystal to powder. A chemical change is a change in which one or more new substances form with different properties: bonds are broken and new bonds form as atoms regroup, so the change is usually difficult or impossible to reverse by simple means. Examples: burning wood (producing ash, carbon dioxide and water vapour), rusting iron (producing iron oxide), frying an egg, milk souring. The deciding question: is a new substance formed? Same substance afterwards — physical; new substance — chemical.

questions.question: List the five observable signs of a chemical change with an example of each, and explain why no single sign is proof on its own.
questions.expected_answer: One: a gas is produced — zinc in dilute acid streams hydrogen bubbles; vinegar on baking soda foams carbon dioxide. Two: a precipitate forms — an insoluble solid appears when two clear solutions react. Three: a permanent colour change — grey iron turns to red-brown rust; copper blackens to copper oxide in a flame. Four: a temperature change the surroundings did not cause — cement warms itself while setting (exothermic), while some reactions absorb energy and turn cold (endothermic). Five: light or sound is emitted — burning magnesium's white flare. No single sign is proof because each can occur without chemistry: bubbles also appear in boiling, which is physical, and physical changes such as melting also involve energy changes. The signs are evidence that raises suspicion; the verdict always rests on whether a new substance has actually formed.

questions.question: A burning candle shows both kinds of change at once, and a braai fire seems to destroy mass. Explain both observations.
questions.expected_answer: At the top of the candle, the flame's heat melts the wax — a physical change: the liquid wax that dribbles down cools and hardens back into the same wax, so no new substance forms. At the wick, the liquid wax burns — a chemical change: the wax combines with oxygen from the air to form carbon dioxide and water vapour, new substances that escape into the room and can never be turned back into wax; this is why the candle gets permanently shorter. The braai fire only seems to destroy mass because the products of combustion — carbon dioxide, water vapour and smoke — escape unweighed, leaving light ash behind. By the law of conservation of mass, atoms are never created or destroyed in a chemical change: if the burning happened in a sealed container and everything, including the oxygen used, were weighed before and after, the total mass would balance exactly. Mass is relocated and regrouped, never lost.
